Magnetism.intro: Magnets exert forces on other magnets and on magnetic materials. Understanding magnetic fields and how they are represented is essential for P7.

sections.title: Magnetic Materials and Poles
points: Magnetic materials: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt
Every magnet has a north and south pole
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract
The Earth has a magnetic field — its geographic north pole is near a magnetic south pole

sections.title: Magnetic Field Lines
points: Show direction and strength of magnetic field
Direction: from north pole to south pole (outside magnet)
Closer lines = stronger field
Never cross each other

sections.title: Induced Magnetism
points: When a magnetic material is placed in a magnetic field it becomes magnetised
Induced magnet always attracted to the magnet causing induction
Iron: loses magnetism easily (soft magnetic material — used in transformers, electromagnets)
Steel: retains magnetism (hard magnetic material — used in permanent magnets)

keyTerms.def: The region around a magnet where magnetic forces act
Magnetism produced in a material when placed in a magnetic field
Magnet that retains its magnetism without an external field

examTips: Magnetic field lines go from N to S outside the magnet.
Iron = soft (temporary magnet). Steel = hard (permanent magnet).
The force between magnets is non-contact — acts at a distance.
commonMistakes: Saying all metals are magnetic — only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic.
Drawing field lines that cross each other — they never cross.

Electromagnetism.intro: An electric current produces a magnetic field. This is the principle behind electromagnets and many electrical devices.

sections.title: Magnetic Field from Current
points: A current-carrying wire produces a circular magnetic field around it
Direction: use right-hand rule (curl fingers around wire — thumb points in current direction, fingers show field direction)
Solenoid (coil of wire): magnetic field like a bar magnet inside
Field strength increases with: more current, more turns in coil, iron core

sections.title: Electromagnets
points: Current through a coil of wire produces a strong magnetic field
Field can be switched on and off (unlike permanent magnets)
Iron core concentrates field — makes it much stronger
Uses: electric bells, scrapyard cranes, MRI scanners, loudspeakers, relays

keyTerms.def: A coil of wire that acts as a magnet when current flows through it
A magnet created by passing an electric current through a coil of wire
Method to find magnetic field direction around a current-carrying wire

examTips: Electromagnet strength increases with: more current, more turns, iron core.
Advantage over permanent magnets: can be switched on/off and varied in strength.
commonMistakes: Saying electromagnets are always stronger than permanent magnets — not necessarily.
Forgetting the iron core magnifies the field — without it, field is much weaker.

Motor Effect.intro: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. This is the motor effect — the principle behind electric motors.

sections.title: The Motor Effect

callout.label: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
callout.text: Point left hand: First finger = Field direction, seCond finger = Current direction, thuMb = Motion (force) direction. FBI — Field, Current, Motion.

points: Force is perpendicular to both current and magnetic field
Force increases with: stronger magnetic field, larger current
Reversing current OR field reverses direction of force

sections.title: The Electric Motor
points: A coil of wire carrying current in a magnetic field experiences forces on opposite sides
Forces in opposite directions → turning effect (torque)
Commutator (split ring) reverses current direction each half turn → keeps motor spinning same way
Brushes maintain electrical contact with commutator

keyTerms.def: Force experienced by a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
Rule for finding force direction: Field (first finger), Current (second), Motion/Force (thumb)
Split ring in a DC motor that reverses current direction each half turn

examTips: Fleming's LEFT-hand rule for MOTOR effect (force/motion). Right-hand rule for generators.
Force is largest when current is perpendicular to the magnetic field.
To reverse motor direction: reverse current OR reverse field (not both).
commonMistakes: Using right-hand rule for motor effect — it's LEFT hand for motors.
Forgetting the commutator's function — without it the motor would oscillate, not rotate continuously.

Generators.intro: Generators use electromagnetic induction to convert kinetic energy into electrical energy. They are the reverse of motors.

sections.title: Electromagnetic Induction
points: Moving a conductor through a magnetic field (or changing field around a conductor) induces a voltage
If circuit is complete: induces a current
This is the generator effect — opposite of the motor effect
Induced voltage increases with: faster movement, stronger field, more turns

sections.title: AC Generator (Alternator)
points: Coil rotates in a magnetic field — continuously changing flux
Produces alternating current (AC) — current reverses direction each half turn
Slip rings and brushes maintain continuous contact
UK mains supply: 230V, 50Hz

sections.title: Microphones and Speakers
points: Microphone: sound waves → diaphragm vibrates → coil moves in field → induces current
Speaker: varying current in coil → force in field → coil/cone vibrates → sound waves

keyTerms.def: Inducing a voltage (and current) by relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field
Producing an electric current from motion in a magnetic field
Current that reverses direction periodically — produced by generators

examTips: Generator is opposite of motor: kinetic → electrical vs electrical → kinetic.
Increase induced voltage: move faster, stronger magnet, more turns, add iron core.
AC generators use slip rings; DC generators use commutator.
commonMistakes: Confusing generators (motion → electricity) with motors (electricity → motion).
Forgetting that stationary conductor in changing field also induces voltage.

Transformers.intro: Transformers change the voltage of an AC supply using electromagnetic induction. They are essential for efficient electricity transmission.

sections.title: How Transformers Work
points: AC in primary coil → changing magnetic field in iron core → induced EMF in secondary coil
Iron core concentrates and transfers magnetic field
Only work with AC — DC produces no changing field, so no induction

callout.label: Turns Ratio Formula
callout.text: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns (Primary voltage ÷ Secondary voltage = Primary turns ÷ Secondary turns). Step up: more turns on secondary. Step down: fewer turns on secondary.

sections.title: Power Transmission
points: Power stations generate at ~25 kV — stepped up to ~400 kV for transmission
High voltage transmission reduces current → reduces power loss (P = I²R)
Step-down transformers reduce voltage to safe levels for homes (230V)
Ideal transformer: power in = power out (Vp × Ip = Vs × Is)

keyTerms.def: Device that changes AC voltage using electromagnetic induction
Increases voltage — more turns on secondary than primary
Decreases voltage — fewer turns on secondary than primary
Ratio of primary to secondary turns — determines voltage change

examTips: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns — cross-multiply to solve for any unknown.
Transformers only work with AC — DC won't induce a current in the secondary.
High voltage transmission reduces power loss: P lost = I²R; less I → less P lost.
commonMistakes: Saying transformers work with DC — they do not; the field must be changing.
Confusing step-up (more secondary turns, higher voltage) with step-down.
